# THEORYs with `tags` `pragmatics`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

| [THEORY-162](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-162.md) | Context change is part of meaning | Heim (1982), [LIT-838](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-838.md); Veltman (1996), [LIT-818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-818.md); Krifka (2024), [LIT-835](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-835.md). Three readings find, each in its own domain, sentences that agree in truth conditions or in the proposition they carry but differ in their effect on a conversational state. The effects are anaphoric potential (Heim), tests rather than information (Veltman), and changing indices rather than eliminating them (Krifka). This is the dynamic view: meaning as context-change potential. It does not say that truth conditions are irrelevant, since each framework recovers them, or that the three formalisms agree with each other. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-172](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-172.md) v5 | Listeners infer speakers choose by informativeness | Frank & Goodman (2012), [LIT-821](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-821.md), read in [NOTE-634](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-634.md): a parameter-free Bayesian listener inverting a size-principle speaker, with a separately measured salience prior, matches mean listener bets over seven context types at r = .99 (.87 without the 0 and 100 predictions), while salience alone correlates at r = .19. Bergen, Goodman & Levy (2012), [LIT-809](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-809.md), read in [NOTE-613](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-613.md): with novel signals and no conventions, listeners read the signal as the object its alternative did not name, and lexical uncertainty derives Horn's mapping. Goodman & Frank (2016), [LIT-816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-816.md), states the framework. | [THEORY-406](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-406.md) v3 | Networked publics collapse audience boundaries | boyd (2008), [LIT-1001](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1001.md), after Meyrowitz (1985), read in part: §1.5, §4.4, the Top Friends passage and every passage on context, segmentation, collision and Goffman in [NOTE-710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-710.md), and Chapters 1, 4 and 7 in full in [NOTE-1432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1432.md) (both Skimmed). | [THEORY-444](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-444.md) v2 | Meaning works through recognized intention | Grice (1957), [LIT-1042](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1042.md), read in full in [NOTE-735](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-735.md). The analysis is reached by counterexamples to weaker conditions (the handkerchief, Herod and Salome, the photograph against the drawing) and stated "roughly". It is an analysis of speaker meaning on an occasion, not of illocutionary acts, and its extension to timeless and sentence meaning is "a first shot" with the red light admitted as awkward. Strawson's watcher case ([LIT-1043](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1043.md)) shows its three intentions are not sufficient. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-472](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-472.md) v4 | Size principle follows from informative speech | Frank, Goodman, Lai and Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-824.md), read in full in [NOTE-627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-627.md). The derivation (utility −D_KL from intended to literal meaning gives P(w) ∝ \|w\|^(−α) for a point referent) is a proof under its assumptions. Learners' bets track the parameter-free inversion at r = .93 on condition means (700 web participants); speakers' tag-word use in free descriptions correlates at r = .19, .51 without colour terms and .02 for them. In these displays the informative-speaker learner and a plain size-principle learner coincide by construction, so the fit does not show that learners reason about the speaker. | Active |
| [THEORY-511](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-511.md) | Non-conventional illocutions are overt intentions | Strawson (1964), [LIT-1043](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1043.md), read in full in [NOTE-736](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-736.md), amending Grice (1957), [LIT-1042](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1042.md). Against Austin, some illocutions need no convention beyond the linguistic; their force is an overt intention meant to be understood, and uptake is the audience's recognition of it, an aim rather than an achievement. Orders fit "with some strain"; verdicts, umpires' calls and marriages do not fit at all. The scheme predicts no non-institutional case in which the overt intention is fixed and the act changes, which gives [QUESTION-073](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-073.md) a definite rival to test. The amended analysis is offered as necessary, not sufficient. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-623](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-623.md) v2 | Language-data contextuality is not secured | Lo, Sadrzadeh & Mansfield (2024), [LIT-844](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-844.md), read in [NOTE-648](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-648.md), and Wang, Sadrzadeh, Abramsky & Cervantes (2021), [LIT-842](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-842.md), read in [NOTE-645](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-645.md). Both readings recomputed the criteria. That 71.1% CbD-contextual measures BERT's uncertainty is [NOTE-648](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-648.md)'s derivation from the stipulated support (CNT1 = 2 − Δ). | [THEORY-665](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-665.md) v2 | Assertion is commitment in deontic scorekeeping | Brandom (1994), [LIT-794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-794.md), skimmed in [NOTE-622](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-622.md): the Preface and the core of chapter 3 only. | [THEORY-1120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1120.md) v3 | COMET tracks pragmatic adequacy at r = 0.81 | Singh et al. (2026), [LIT-1817](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1817.md), read in [NOTE-1345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1345.md). On 416 outputs (104 items × 4 models), wmt22 COMET correlates with 1–5 pragmatic-adequacy scores at Pearson 0.813, Spearman 0.860; XCOMET ρ 0.792, MetricX ρ 0.788 (Table 3). Four hand-picked outputs scored 0.65–0.86 by COMET and 1–2 by the rater. Each language had one rater, so there is no reliability against which to read 0.81, and the claim that metrics fail "especially for implicature and deixis" rests on per-phenomenon differences of 0.1 or less. | Active |
| [THEORY-1131](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1131.md) | LLMs choose Indic pragmatic readings, lean literal | Singh et al. (2026), [LIT-1817](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1817.md), read in [NOTE-1345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1345.md) from the Findings of EMNLP 2026 PDF. MCQ beat NLI in 20 of 20 model–language pairs (recomputed). 59.1% of wrong MCQ answers took the literal distractor, against 33.3% by chance, and 53.8% of Contradiction items were labelled Entailment. The gold answers are each language's one item author's reading, cells hold 5–16 items, and the MCQ and NLI sets are different items. | [THEORY-1148](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1148.md) | Judges agree moderately on pragmatic similarity | Ward and Marco (2024), [LIT-1812](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1812.md), read in [NOTE-1338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1338.md) from the LREC-COLING 2024 PDF. Over 693 seed/re-enactment pairs in three sessions, mean pairwise Pearson agreement was 0.45, 0.72 and 0.66 (Table 2), and 0.80 in Session 2 when lexically different pairs were left out (p. 160). The Spearman–Brown reliability of the panel means, 0.88–0.96, is my computation.
